I've found the Perneger 1998 article. Here's a summary of the key arguments presented in "What's wrong with Bonferroni adjustments":

## Main Arguments

Perneger advances the view that Bonferroni adjustments are, at best, unnecessary and, at worst, deleterious to sound statistical inference.

## Key Problems Identified

The Bonferroni method is concerned with the general null hypothesis (that all null hypotheses are true simultaneously), which is rarely of interest or use to researchers. The main weakness is that the interpretation of a finding depends on the number of other tests performed. The likelihood of type II errors is also increased, so that truly important differences are deemed non-significant.

## Recommended Alternative

Simply describing what tests of significance have been performed, and why, is generally the best way of dealing with multiple comparisons. Additionally, the integration of prior beliefs with evidence is best achieved by Bayesian methods, not by Bonferroni adjustments.

## Conclusion

Bonferroni adjustments have, at best, limited applications in biomedical research, and should not be used when assessing evidence about specific hypotheses.

The article was published on April 18, 1998, in the BMJ (volume 316, pages 1236-1238).

Based on the search results, here's information about the Simmons et al. 2011 paper:

## Overview

The paper "False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant" was published in Psychological Science, Volume 22, Issue 11, pages 1359-1366 in 2011, by Joseph P. Simmons from The Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, Leif D. Nelson from the Haas School of Business at UC Berkeley, and Uri Simonsohn from The Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania.

## Main Findings

The paper presents computer simulations and a pair of actual experiments that demonstrate how unacceptably easy it is to accumulate (and report) statistically significant evidence for a false hypothesis. 

The authors show that despite empirical psychologists' nominal endorsement of a low rate of false-positive findings (≤ .05), flexibility in data collection, analysis, and reporting dramatically increases actual false-positive rates. In many cases, a researcher is more likely to falsely find evidence that an effect exists than to correctly find evidence that it does not.

## Proposed Solutions

The authors suggest a simple, low-cost, and straightforwardly effective disclosure-based solution to this problem, which involves six concrete requirements for authors and four guidelines for reviewers, all of which impose a minimal burden on the publication process.

This paper has become highly influential in highlighting the problem of false positives in psychological research and is a cornerstone work in discussions about research reproducibility and methodology.

Based on the search results, I found the paper you're looking for:

**"Rethinking Word Similarity: Semantic Similarity through Classification Confusion"** by Kaitlyn Zhou, Haishan Gao, Sarah Li Chen, Dan Edelstein, Dan Jurafsky, and Chen Shani was published at NAACL 2025.

The paper addresses limitations of traditional similarity methods based on cosine similarity between word embeddings, which cannot capture the context-dependent, asymmetrical, polysemous nature of semantic similarity. The authors propose a new measure of similarity called Word Confusion that reframes semantic similarity in terms of feature-based classification confusion.

Word Confusion is inspired by Tversky's suggestion that similarity features be chosen dynamically. The approach trains a classifier to map contextual embeddings to word identities and uses the classifier confusion (the probability of choosing a confounding word instead of the correct target word) as a measure of similarity.

Their method is comparable to cosine similarity in matching human similarity judgments across several datasets (MEN, WordSim353, and SimLex), and can measure similarity using predetermined features of interest. The researchers demonstrate their model's ability to make use of dynamic features by applying it to test a hypothesis about changes in the 18th century meaning of the French word "révolution" from popular to state action during the French Revolution.

## Label Confusion Learning to Enhance Text Classification Models

The paper proposes a novel Label Confusion Model (LCM) as an enhancement component to text classification models that can learn label confusion to capture semantic overlap among labels by calculating the similarity between instance and labels during training and generate a better label distribution to replace the original one-hot label vector.

**Authors:** The research was conducted by Biyang Guo, Songqiao Han, Xiao Han, Hailiang Huang, and Ting Lu from the AI Lab at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics.

I found the research paper you're looking for. Here's what I found:

CHiLS: Zero-Shot Image Classification with Hierarchical Label Sets was authored by Zachary Novack, Julian McAuley, Zachary Lipton, and Saurabh Garg and published at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) in 2023.

CHiLS is an alternative strategy for zero-shot classification specifically designed for datasets with implicit semantic hierarchies. The method proceeds in three steps: (i) for each class, produce a set of subclasses, using either existing label hierarchies or by querying GPT-3; (ii) perform the standard zero-shot CLIP procedure as though these subclasses were the labels of interest; (iii) map the predicted subclass back to its parent to produce the final prediction.

Across numerous datasets with underlying hierarchical structure, CHiLS leads to improved accuracy in situations both with and without ground-truth hierarchical information. CHiLS is simple to implement within existing zero-shot pipelines and requires no additional training cost.

The code is available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/acmi-lab/CHILS

Based on the search results, here's what I found about ZERONER for ACL 2025:

## ZeroNER Overview

ZeroNER is a description-driven framework that enhances hard zero-shot NER in low-resource settings. By leveraging general-domain annotations and entity type descriptions with LLM supervision, ZeroNER enables a BERT-based student model to successfully identify unseen entity types.

## Key Results

Evaluated on three real-world benchmarks, ZeroNER consistently outperforms LLMs by up to 16% in F1 score, and surpasses lightweight baselines that use type names alone.

## Key Innovation

The framework addresses an important limitation in existing zero-shot NER approaches. Existing zero-shot methods predominantly adopt a relaxed definition of the term with potential leakage issues and rely on entity type names for generalization, overlooking the value of richer descriptions for disambiguation.

## Publication Details

ZeroNER was published in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025, pages 15594–15616, Vienna, Austria. The research was conducted by authors from the University of Bologna and IBM Research Europe, Dublin.
